opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the really interesting puzzles. My take is that it comes down to what the data actually represents. Text isn't just some random signal about the world. It's something people produced specifically to communicate the things they thought were important. When you train a model to predict the next word, you're essentially training it to reconstruct the reasoning, the abstractions, the decisions of the person who wrote it. Language is already a highly compressed, highly curated representation of the parts of the world humans care about.

Video is very different. A video is a raw recording of physical reality, and most of the bits in it are, frankly, not that important. The exact texture of the leaves blowing in the background, the precise way light reflects off a table: a video prediction model has to spend a huge amount of capacity modeling that stuff, because that's what the loss tells it to do. Nothing in the objective says, "Focus on the part where the person decides to pick up the cup, and on why they did it." So you can get a model that's extremely good at producing visually plausible pixels without necessarily extracting the abstractions you'd want for reasoning or for acting.

Here's one way I like to put it. With language models, you're getting a kind of shortcut: you're piggybacking on all the work humans already did to figure out what matters and to put it into words. With video you don't get that shortcut. The model has to discover for itself which variables are the important ones, and pure prediction is a pretty weak signal for that.

That's actually part of why I'm excited about robotics and about learning from embodied interaction. When an agent is actually trying to accomplish something, the task itself tells you what matters. If I'm trying to fold a shirt, I need to care about where the corners of the shirt are, and I don't need to care about the wallpaper. So I think the path to getting broadly useful intelligence out of the physical world is probably not just "predict the next frame really well." It's more about combining that rich perceptual data with goals and actions, so that the learning is grounded in what's relevant for doing things, and probably leveraging the abstractions we already get from language models on top of that.

r001.rationale: The response says video prediction spends substantial capacity modeling details such as leaf texture and light reflections before focusing on human-relevant decisions.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a highly compressed, curated representation of the parts of the world people care about.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's a little bit of a puzzle, and I don't think anyone fully understands it. But I have a hypothesis, and the hypothesis is basically about what is in the data.

When you train a language model on text, the text was produced by humans, and humans are intelligent agents. So the text is not just a record of events, it's a record of what people thought about, how they reasoned, what they concluded, and it's already compressed. Somebody took the messy, high-dimensional world, extracted the parts that mattered, and wrote those down. So in a sense, language models are getting the benefit of a lot of cognitive work that was done for them. The abstraction has already been performed by a person. The model is predicting the output of a thinking process, and if you get good enough at predicting the output of a thinking process, you end up having to represent a lot of that process.

Video is the opposite. Video is raw. It's a record of the physical world, and the physical world doesn't care which parts are important. If you're trying to predict the next frame, the overwhelming majority of the bits in that frame are things like how the leaves move in the wind, or the texture of the carpet, or sensor noise. Those bits are extremely hard to predict and almost completely useless for making decisions. So you can spend an enormous amount of capacity getting very good at the stuff that doesn't matter, and the question of "what is the actual latent structure here that I should be modeling" is left entirely to the model to figure out. With text, that question was mostly answered by the person who wrote it.

There's a second piece, which I think is related, which is that in text, the gap between the representation and the thing you want to do with it is very small. If you want a model to answer a question, it reads a question and produces an answer, and that's the same modality as the training data. With video, even if you had a perfect video model, there's still a big gap between predicting pixels and actually doing something in the world. You need to turn that into actions, into decisions. And that's a lot of what we've been working on in robotics, trying to close that gap.

So I don't think it's that video is a bad signal. I actually think there's an enormous amount of information about the world in video that is simply not in text, things about physics, about how objects behave, about what happens when you push on something. Text doesn't really tell you that, or it tells you in a very impoverished way. But extracting it requires the model to do the abstraction itself, and we haven't been as good at setting up objectives that force that abstraction to happen. Next-token prediction on text sort of gets it for free. Next-frame prediction on video doesn't. And I suspect the eventual answer is going to look less like "predict video better" and more like some combination of video with language, with actions, with some kind of objective that tells the model which parts of the world are worth paying attention to.

r001.rationale: It says video prediction can consume enormous capacity on hard-to-predict, decision-irrelevant details such as moving leaves, carpet texture, and sensor noise before modeling useful latent structure.

r002.rationale: It describes human-written text as already compressed: people extract what matters from the world, so the representation carries human-performed abstraction.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that predicting video forces you to solve a lot of problems that aren’t necessarily the problems we care about for intelligence. If you’re predicting text, a lot of the details have already been abstracted away by the person who produced the text. They’ve decided what matters and expressed it in words. In video, you have to figure out that abstraction yourself, while also predicting things like textures, lighting, and exactly how the camera is moving.

Imagine watching somebody trying to open a door. You might care about whether the door is locked, whether they need to push or pull, or whether they have the right key. But most of the pixels are about other things. You could improve your video prediction loss substantially by getting those other things right without learning very much about how to open doors.

That doesn’t mean video prediction can’t produce useful intelligence. I think it probably can. But there’s a question of what makes learning focus on the right things. For an agent, taking actions and seeing their consequences gives you a way to discover which distinctions matter. Whether the door is locked makes a big difference to what you can do next, even if it makes almost no difference to what the current image looks like.

So I’d distinguish learning to predict what you’re going to see from learning a model that’s useful for deciding what to do. Those are related, but I don’t think we should assume that making progress on the first automatically gives us the second.

r001.rationale: The response says video models must predict textures, lighting, and camera motion, and can reduce loss by getting those details right without learning much about the human-relevant task of opening a door.

r002.rationale: It explains that the person producing text has already decided what matters and expressed it in words, so text has already abstracted away many details.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that predicting text is already a task that’s very closely aligned with the things we want an intelligent system to do. If you’re predicting an explanation of how to solve a math problem, then doing a good job of prediction requires figuring out something about the math. A lot of the work of deciding what matters has already been done by the person who wrote the text.

With video, the prediction problem includes an enormous amount of stuff that we don’t necessarily care about. What’s the exact texture of this surface? How does the lighting change? Which way does a leaf move? Those are legitimate parts of predicting the next frame, but you could spend a tremendous amount of capacity getting them right without learning how to accomplish a task.

And there’s a distinction between predicting what happens and understanding what you can make happen. If I watch somebody interacting with an object, I might learn something about how that object behaves. But what I really need for control is: if I take this particular action, what will happen next? In ordinary video, the actions aren’t necessarily labeled, and you don’t get to try an alternative action and observe the result. So learning something that supports decision-making is a less direct consequence of the prediction objective.

That doesn’t mean video prediction can’t work. I think it could be an important ingredient. But I’d be careful about assuming that the recipe is simply to replace text tokens with video tokens and scale it up. You probably want some combination of prediction, actions, and interaction that makes the model learn the aspects of the world that are useful for actually doing things.

r001.rationale: The response says video prediction can spend “a tremendous amount of capacity” modeling details like texture, lighting, and leaf movement without learning how to accomplish a task.

r002.rationale: It explains that text is closely aligned with useful tasks and that the writer has already done much of the work of deciding what matters, conveying that text abstracts toward human-relevant information.
